lessons.title: Study Session 1: Mapping a Manual Process Clearly Before Automating It

blocks.text: Introduction Erasto Shikongo processes leave requests for a district agriculture extension office in Rundu, and had built an automation to route each request from a staff member to a supervisor and then to the records office, based on how he remembered the process working, only for the automation to jam completely the first time a request arrived while a supervisor was already on leave. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about automating a process without first reviewing whether it should be redesigned. Distinguish a clearly mapped process, including its exceptions, from one built on an assumed mental model. Apply a method for mapping a process's actual steps, decision points and exceptions before automating it. Recognise when a process needs redesign rather than straightforward automation. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 An Automation Built From Memory, Not From the Real Process Erasto Shikongo's district agriculture extension office in Rundu needed leave requests routed automatically from a staff member to their supervisor and then to the records office, and Erasto built the automation based on how he remembered the approval chain working. The first time a request arrived while the relevant supervisor was already on leave themselves, a situation Erasto had never actually accounted for, the automation had nowhere to send the request and simply stopped, leaving the staff member's leave unapproved for a week. 2.2 What Research Found About Automating a Process Without Redesigning It The management researcher Michael Hammer argued in a widely read 1990 Harvard Business Review article that automating an existing process without first questioning whether that process should be redesigned tends to lock the process's flaws in place, sometimes making them more expensive to fix later. His central claim was that organisations should reexamine a process's actual purpose and structure before applying technology to speed it up. 2.3 Mapping a Process's Real Steps, Decisions and Exceptions Writing Down Every Branch a Process Can Actually Take Listing not only a process's usual path but every branch it can realistically take, including who covers a decision when the usual decision-maker is unavailable, surfaces the exceptions that an automation built from memory alone tends to miss. Asking Whether a Step Still Deserves to Exist Questioning whether each step in a mapped process still serves a real purpose, instead of automating a step purely out of habit, prevents an automation from quietly preserving an outdated way of working. 2.4 Key Practices Write out a process's usual path and every realistic exception before automating any of it. Identify who or what covers a decision when the usual decision-maker is unavailable. Question whether each mapped step still serves a real purpose before automating it. Walk a mapped process past someone who performs it regularly, checking for missed branches. 2.5 A Worked Example: Erasto's Full Process Map After the failed leave request, Erasto sat with two colleagues who actually handled approvals day to day and wrote out every branch the process could take, including a supervisor being unavailable, a request needing backdating, and a request spanning two different approval periods. The rebuilt automation, now routing to a named backup approver whenever the primary supervisor's own leave was on record, handled the next unusual request without any manual intervention. Requests that once required Erasto to step in manually now cleared the approval chain on their own in every case the office actually encountered across the rest of that season. Erasto's original automation had not been built carelessly. It had been built from a memory of the process rather than the process itself, and only sitting with the people who actually ran it ever surfaced the branch that had been missing. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Building an automation directly from a personal memory of how a process works, without checking that memory against the people who actually perform the process, risks missing exceptions that only surface once the automation is already relied upon, which is what left Erasto's first version jammed for a week. Automating a step without questioning whether it still serves a purpose can lock an outdated habit into a system that is now harder to change than the original manual process was. 2.7 A Remembered Process and a Mapped Process Are Different Things Erasto had genuinely understood the leave approval process well enough to explain it to a new colleague in conversation. That understanding turned out to be incomplete in a way conversation alone never revealed, and only writing out every branch with the people who ran the process day to day ever closed the gap. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to map a process's real steps and exceptions before automating any part of it. Study Session 2 turns from mapping a process to choosing the no-code platform actually suited to automating it.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a manual process at your own workplace. Could you name every exception it has, or only its usual path? 2. Map one real process's full set of steps and exceptions with a colleague who performs it regularly, before automating any part of it. Practical Output: Practical Output A written process map for one real recurring task, showing its usual path and at least three realistic exceptions, drafted with input from someone who performs the task regularly. 7.0 References and Further Reading Hammer, M. (1990). Reengineering work: Don't automate, obliterate. Harvard Business Review, 68(4), 104 to 112. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Psalm 127:1, on labouring in vain to build a house without the Lord's help. Qur'an, Surah Al-Kahf 18:104, on effort being lost while thinking oneself to be doing good work.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 2: Choosing the Right No-Code Platform for a Specific Task

blocks.text: Introduction Mariam Youssouf, who is deaf and coordinates communication mainly through text, schedules volunteers for a community health outreach programme in Mutsamudu, and had spent three weeks building a volunteer reminder automation on a platform a colleague recommended, before discovering the platform could only send app notifications and had no way to reach the SMS-only phones most of her volunteers actually used. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about comparing no-code and low-code development platforms. Distinguish a platform feature that actually matters for a task from one that does not. Apply a method for evaluating a no-code platform against a task's real requirements before building on it. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 Three Weeks Building on the Wrong Platform Mariam Youssouf's community health outreach programme in Mutsamudu needed volunteers reminded automatically ahead of each outreach day, and Mariam chose a no-code platform a colleague had recommended without checking its specific capabilities against what her volunteers actually used. Three weeks into building the reminder automation, Mariam discovered the platform could only deliver notifications through its own app, with no way to reach the basic SMS-only phones that most of her volunteers actually carried. 2.2 What Research Found About Comparing No-Code Platforms Alessio Sahay and colleagues published a 2020 paper at the Euromicro Conference on Software Engineering and Advanced Applications addressing how difficult it is to choose among the large number of available low-code and no-code development platforms without a structured comparison method. Their finding was that platforms vary substantially in ways not obvious from marketing descriptions alone, and that decision-makers evaluating them without a clear framework often struggle to identify which differences actually matter for their specific task. 2.3 Evaluating a Platform Against a Task's Real Requirements Listing a Task's Non-Negotiable Requirements First Writing down exactly what a task requires, which communication channels it must reach, which apps it must connect to, before looking at any specific platform prevents a platform's attractive but irrelevant features from distracting from what actually matters. Testing a Platform's Actual Capability, Not Its Marketing Description Building a small test case on a platform before committing to it fully, specifically testing the exact requirement most likely to be a problem, catches a capability gap before weeks of work have already gone into the wrong tool. 2.4 Key Practices List a task's non-negotiable requirements before evaluating any specific platform. Test a platform's actual capability against the task's hardest requirement before committing to it. Avoid choosing a platform solely because a colleague recommended it for a different task. Confirm a platform can reach every channel or app the task actually depends on. Note down why a given platform was chosen for a given task, for future reference. 2.5 A Worked Example: Mariam's Platform Requirements List Before starting again, Mariam wrote out exactly what the reminder automation needed, reaching SMS-only phones being the single non-negotiable requirement, and tested three platforms against that one requirement before building anything further. Only one of the three could actually send SMS messages directly, and Mariam rebuilt the reminder automation on that platform in under a week using much of the logic she had already worked out. The volunteer outreach programme's attendance improved noticeably once reminders actually reached the phones volunteers carried, rather than an app most of them had never installed. Mariam's first platform choice had not been an unreasonable one to consider. No one had checked it against the one requirement that mattered most, and only writing that requirement down before choosing ever prevented the same mistake twice. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Choosing a no-code platform because a colleague recommended it, without checking that platform's specific capabilities against the current task's real requirements, risks weeks of work built on a tool that cannot actually do what the task needs, which is what happened with Mariam's first attempt. Evaluating a platform by its marketing description rather than by a small direct test of its hardest requirement can hide a capability gap until it is expensive to discover. 2.7 A Recommended Platform Is Not the Same as a Suitable One The platform Mariam's colleague recommended had worked well for that colleague's own task, and the recommendation had been made in good faith. A platform's success on one task said nothing about its fit for a different task with different requirements, and only testing it against Mariam's own specific requirement ever revealed the gap. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to evaluate a no-code platform against a task's real requirements before building on it. Study Session 3 moves from choosing a platform to actually constructing a trigger-action automation and matching data fields correctly between two connected apps.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a no-code platform you have chosen for a task. Was it evaluated against the task's actual requirements, or chosen for another reason? 2. List one real task's non-negotiable requirements and test at least two platforms against the hardest one before choosing. Practical Output: Practical Output A short requirements list for one real automation task, with at least two platforms tested against its hardest non-negotiable requirement and a documented choice. 7.0 References and Further Reading Sahay, A., Indamutsa, A., Di Ruscio, D., & Pierantonio, A. (2020). Supporting the understanding and comparison of low-code development platforms. Proceedings of the 46th Euromicro Conference on Software Engineering and Advanced Applications (SEAA 2020), 171 to 178. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Proverbs 19:2, on the soul being without knowledge not being good, and one who hastens with his feet sinning. Qur'an, Surah Al-Alaq 96:5, on taught man that which he knew not.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 3: Building a Trigger-Action Automation and Matching Data Fields Between Two Apps

blocks.text: Introduction Steevy Mba manages restocking alerts for a hardware supply business in Franceville, and built an automation meant to message a supplier whenever an item's stock fell below twenty units, only to discover after a month that not one alert had ever fired, because the inventory app recorded quantities as text like twelve boxes rather than a plain number the automation's trigger could actually compare. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about the practical challenges practitioners face building low-code automations. Distinguish a data field correctly matched between two apps from one silently mismatched. Apply a method for testing that data actually transfers correctly between connected apps. Recognise when a task has exceeded what a no-code platform can reliably do. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 A Month of Silence From an Automation That Never Fired Steevy Mba's hardware supply business in Franceville needed a supplier messaged automatically whenever any item's stock fell below twenty units, and Steevy built a trigger-action automation connecting the inventory spreadsheet app to a messaging app to do exactly that. A full month passed without a single alert firing, even though at least six items had genuinely dropped below the threshold, and only a manual stock check uncovered the problem. 2.2 What Research Found About Low-Code Development's Practical Challenges Yajing Luo and colleagues surveyed developer discussion on Stack Overflow and Reddit for a 2021 paper presented at the International Symposium on Empirical Software Engineering and Measurement, examining what practitioners actually struggle with when building low-code and no-code automations. Among their findings, practitioners frequently reported difficulty with data handling between connected systems, along with debugging problems that were often hard to diagnose because the underlying logic was hidden behind a visual interface. 2.3 Matching Data Fields Correctly Between Connected Apps Checking What Format a Field Actually Stores, Not What It Displays Opening a connected app's raw field, rather than trusting how a value appears on screen, reveals whether a quantity is actually stored as a plain number the automation's trigger can compare, or as text that happens to look similar. Sending a Deliberate Test Value Through the Whole Chain Entering one clearly identifiable test value into the source app and confirming it arrives correctly at every later step of the automation actually proves the fields are matched, instead of assuming a connection labelled correctly must be working correctly. 2.4 Key Practices Check a connected field's actual stored format, not just how it appears on screen. Send a deliberate, identifiable test value through the entire automation before trusting it. Confirm a threshold comparison is actually comparing numbers, not text that resembles numbers. Recognise when a task's data handling needs exceed what the chosen platform can reliably support. 2.5 A Worked Example: Steevy's Field-by-Field Test Steevy opened the inventory app's raw field settings and found that stock quantities were stored as text combining a number and a unit, twelve boxes rather than 12, which meant the automation's numeric threshold comparison had been evaluating nothing meaningful since the day it was built. Steevy added a step converting the field to a plain number before the comparison, then sent a deliberate test entry of five units through the full chain to confirm the alert fired correctly. The supplier received a correctly triggered restocking alert within a day of the fix, for the first genuinely low-stock item recorded since the automation had been built. The automation's trigger logic itself had been built correctly from the start. The problem sat entirely in the data feeding that logic, which was never in a format it could actually use, and only checking the field's real stored format ever surfaced the mismatch. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Trusting that a connected field is passing the right kind of data simply because it displays correctly on screen, without checking its actual stored format, can leave an automation's core comparison silently comparing the wrong kind of value, exactly what happened with Steevy's stock quantities for a full month. Building an automation's full trigger-action chain without sending a deliberate test value through it end to end makes a data mismatch invisible until a real case fails to trigger anything at all. 2.7 Correct Logic on Incorrect Data Still Produces Nothing Steevy's threshold comparison logic, once examined, turned out to have been built correctly from the very beginning. Correct logic had done nothing useful while the data feeding it remained in the wrong format, and only tracing a test value through the full chain ever exposed exactly where the mismatch sat. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to match data fields carefully between connected apps and test an automation's full chain with a deliberate value. Study Session 4 turns from building an automation correctly to testing it against the edge cases it will eventually meet before trusting it to run unattended.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of an automation you have built or used. Have you checked a connected field's actual stored format, or only trusted how it looks on screen? 2. Send one deliberate, identifiable test value through a real automation's full chain and confirm it arrives correctly at every step. Practical Output: Practical Output A field-by-field test record for one real trigger-action automation, showing a deliberate test value traced through every step of the chain. 7.0 References and Further Reading Luo, Y., Liang, P., Wang, C., Shahin, M., & Zhan, J. (2021). Characteristics and challenges of low-code development: The practitioners' perspective. Proceedings of the 15th ACM/IEEE International Symposium on Empirical Software Engineering and Measurement (ESEM 2021). Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: 1 Corinthians 3:10, on taking heed how one builds upon a foundation already laid. Qur'an, Surah Al-Mulk 67:3, on there being no inconsistency in what is well made.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

quiz.q: Erasto's automation jammed the first time a request arrived while a supervisor was on leave. What did this reveal?
options: The agriculture extension office's approval chain was poorly designed
An automation built from a remembered version of a process can miss exceptions the real process actually contains
Leave requests should never be automated
Erasto had entered the wrong supervisor's name into the system
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Mapping a Manual Process Clearly Before Automating It) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to Hammer's 1990 research, what happens when an existing process is automated without first being redesigned?
options: The process automatically improves regardless of its original design
The process's existing flaws tend to be locked in place, sometimes at greater cost to fix later
Automation always removes the need for any human decision-making
Redesigning a process before automating it is unnecessary
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Mapping a Manual Process Clearly Before Automating It) before continuing.

quiz.q: What does this session recommend doing before automating a mapped process's steps?
options: Automating every step exactly as currently performed without question
Questioning whether each step still serves a real purpose
Skipping any consultation with people who perform the process
Assuming the process has no exceptions worth mapping
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Mapping a Manual Process Clearly Before Automating It) before continuing.

quiz.q: Mariam discovered, three weeks into building, that her chosen platform could not reach her volunteers' SMS-only phones. What did this reveal?
options: Community health programmes should not use automation platforms
Choosing a platform without checking its capabilities against the task's real requirements risks weeks of wasted work
SMS reminders are always less effective than app notifications
Mariam's volunteers had provided incorrect phone numbers
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Choosing the Right No-Code Platform for a Specific Task) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to Sahay and colleagues' 2020 research, what makes choosing among no-code and low-code platforms difficult?
options: There are too few platforms available to compare
Platforms vary substantially in ways not obvious from marketing descriptions, without a structured comparison method
All no-code platforms are functionally identical to one another
Platform capabilities never change once a task begins
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Choosing the Right No-Code Platform for a Specific Task) before continuing.

quiz.q: What does this session recommend doing before evaluating any specific platform?
options: Nothing; the first available platform should always be used
Listing the task's non-negotiable requirements
Assuming every platform can meet every possible requirement
Choosing based solely on which platform is most popular
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Choosing the Right No-Code Platform for a Specific Task) before continuing.

lessons.title: Study Session 4: Testing an Automation Against Edge Cases Before Trusting It Unattended

blocks.text: Introduction Yohannes Habte builds customs paperwork automatically from shipment records for a logistics office in Massawa, and let the automation run unsupervised after it produced clean paperwork for the first ten shipments he tested, all single-item domestic deliveries, only for it to generate blank documents for the first international shipment with multiple items that actually came through. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about over-reliance on automation once it has worked a few times. Distinguish an automation tested against realistic edge cases from one trusted after a clean run. Apply a method for testing a new automation against edge cases before allowing it to run unattended. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 Ten Clean Runs and One Blank Document Yohannes Habte's logistics office in Massawa needed customs paperwork drafted automatically from each new shipment record, and Yohannes tested the automation against ten sample shipments before letting it run without supervision. Every one of those ten had been a single-item domestic delivery, and the first genuinely different case to arrive, an international shipment carrying four separate items, produced a blank customs document with no error message explaining why. 2.2 What Research Found About Over-Reliance on Automation Raja Parasuraman and Victor Riley reviewed decades of human factors research in a 1997 Human Factors paper, examining how people actually use, misuse, disuse and abuse automated systems. One of their central findings was that people frequently come to over-rely on an automation once it has performed correctly a number of times, reducing the ongoing monitoring that would otherwise catch the automation's eventual failures. 2.3 Testing an Automation Against Realistic Edge Cases Deliberately Choosing Test Cases Unlike the Easy Ones Selecting test cases specifically because they differ from the simplest, most common scenario, multiple items instead of one, an unusual destination, a missing optional field, is what genuinely shows whether an automation can handle the full range of real situations it will eventually meet. Treating a Clean Run of Easy Cases as Incomplete Testing Recognising that ten successful runs of the same simple scenario provide far less confidence than a handful of runs covering genuinely different scenarios keeps a learner from mistaking repetition for actual coverage. 2.4 Key Practices Choose test cases specifically because they differ from the simplest, most common scenario. Treat repeated success on the same easy case as incomplete testing, not proof of readiness. Test at least one case involving a missing or unusual value before trusting an automation. Watch a new automation's first several unattended real runs closely before stepping back fully. 2.5 A Worked Example: Yohannes's Edge Case Test Set After the blank document, Yohannes built a deliberate set of five test shipments covering multiple items, an international destination, and a shipment missing an optional weight field, and ran all five through the automation before trusting it again. Two of the five produced errors immediately, revealing exactly where the paperwork template's logic broke down for anything beyond the single-item domestic case. Once those two failures were fixed and retested, every one of the five edge cases produced correctly formatted paperwork, and the automation handled the office's actual mix of shipment types without further blank documents for the rest of that quarter. The ten clean early runs had not been misleading in themselves. They had simply all tested the same narrow situation, and only deliberately testing situations unlike that one ever revealed what the automation could not yet do. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Trusting a new automation to run unattended after several successful runs of the same simple scenario, without testing scenarios that differ from it, leaves an automation vulnerable to exactly the kind of unusual case it was never actually checked against, which is what produced Yohannes's blank customs document. Treating repeated success as proof of readiness, rather than as evidence limited to the specific case being repeated, tends to be reduced monitoring exactly at the point real edge cases begin to appear. 2.7 Ten Successes on the Same Case Is Not Ten Kinds of Evidence Yohannes's automation had genuinely produced correct paperwork on every one of its first ten runs. All ten had tested the identical narrow situation, and only building a set of deliberately different test cases ever showed where that narrow success actually stopped. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to test a new automation against deliberately chosen edge cases before trusting it to run unattended. Study Session 5 turns from testing before trusting to recognising when an automation already running has silently broken.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of an automation you have trusted after a few successful runs. Did those runs test genuinely different scenarios, or the same one repeated? 2. Build a set of at least three deliberately different edge cases for one real automation and test it against all three before trusting it unattended. Practical Output: Practical Output An edge-case test set for one real automation, showing at least three deliberately different test scenarios and their results. 7.0 References and Further Reading Parasuraman, R., & Riley, V. (1997). Humans and automation: Use, misuse, disuse, abuse. Human Factors, 39(2), 230 to 253. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Deuteronomy 13:14, on enquiring, making search and asking diligently. Qur'an, Surah Yunus 10:36, on most people following nothing but conjecture, which avails nothing against the truth.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 5: Recognising When an Automation Has Silently Broken

blocks.text: Introduction Isatou Ceesay looks after her mother in the evenings after her shifts and manages appointment reminders for a small clinic in Basse Santa Su through an automation that texts patients ahead of each visit, and only discovered, three weeks after the clinic's booking app changed its date format, that the reminders had been going out with garbled or missing appointment dates the entire time. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about the fragility of automations built on top of other systems' interfaces. Distinguish a silent failure, one producing no error message, from a visible one. Apply a method for checking an automation's actual output against what it should have produced. Recognise the warning signs that an automation has drifted from correct behaviour. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 Three Weeks of Reminders With the Wrong Dates Isatou Ceesay's small clinic in Basse Santa Su relied on an automation that texted each patient a reminder ahead of their appointment, pulling the date directly from the clinic's booking app. When that booking app updated and quietly changed how it recorded appointment dates, the automation kept running without any error, but the dates it inserted into outgoing texts became garbled or blank, and nobody at the clinic noticed until a patient called asking why her reminder listed no date at all. 2.2 What Research Found About Automations Built on Other Systems' Interfaces Wil van der Aalst, Martin Bichler and Andreas Heinzl described, in a 2018 editorial for Business and Information Systems Engineering, how automations that operate by reading and acting on another system's interface are inherently fragile to small changes in that interface. Their central point was that such automations can fail the moment an underlying app changes something as minor as a date format or a field's position, often without producing any visible error at all. 2.3 Checking an Automation's Actual Output Against What It Should Produce Periodically Reading a Sample of an Automation's Real Output Actually reading a handful of an automation's recent real outputs, not just confirming that it ran without an error message, is what catches a silent failure that produces something technically completed but practically wrong. Watching for a Downstream Result That Does Not Match Expectations Noticing a pattern in downstream results, patients missing appointments more often than usual, that does not obviously trace back to the automation is often the first real signal that something upstream has quietly stopped working correctly. 2.4 Key Practices Periodically read a sample of an automation's actual recent output, not just its completion status. Watch downstream results for patterns that suggest an automation is no longer working as expected. Check an automation's output again after any connected app updates or changes its interface. Set a simple, regular reminder to spot-check a critical automation's real output. 2.5 A Worked Example: Isatou's Output Spot-Check After the patient's call, Isatou began reading a sample of five outgoing reminder texts each week rather than only checking that the automation had run, and immediately found that the date field had been blank or garbled since the booking app's update three weeks earlier. Isatou adjusted the automation to match the app's new date format and resumed the weekly spot-check as a standing habit. Missed appointments traced back to reminder confusion dropped sharply within two weeks of the fix, and the weekly spot-check caught a second, smaller formatting issue the following month before any patient was affected. The automation had never actually stopped running during those three weeks. It had simply been producing output that looked complete while containing nothing useful, and only reading the real output directly ever revealed that. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Confirming only that an automation completed without an error message, rather than actually reading a sample of what it produced, can leave a silent failure running undetected for weeks, exactly what happened with Isatou's reminder texts. Failing to recheck an automation's output after a connected app updates its interface risks exactly the kind of quiet breakage that formatting or field changes tend to cause. 2.7 Completing Without Error Is Not the Same as Working Correctly Isatou's reminder automation had reported no error across the whole three weeks its dates were garbled. The absence of an error had never meant the output was actually correct, and only reading the real texts patients received ever showed the difference between the two. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to check an automation's real output directly rather than trusting its completion status alone. Study Session 6 closes this course by turning to how a growing set of automations is documented, owned and governed over time.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of an automation you rely on. Have you read a sample of its actual recent output, or only confirmed that it completed? 2. Read five recent real outputs from one real automation and compare them directly against what they should have contained. Practical Output: Practical Output An output spot-check log for one real automation, showing at least five recent outputs read directly and compared against expected results. 7.0 References and Further Reading van der Aalst, W.M.P., Bichler, M., & Heinzl, A. (2018). Robotic process automation. Business & Information Systems Engineering, 60(4), 269 to 272. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Luke 12:2, on nothing being covered that will not be revealed, nor hidden that will not be known. Qur'an, Surah Al-Adiyat 100:10, on that which is in the breasts being made apparent.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 6: Maintaining and Governing a Growing Set of Automations Over Time

blocks.text: Introduction Arlindo Nsue built automation after automation for an NGO's finance team in Malabo over nearly two years, until a new finance director's simple question, how many automations are currently running and who is responsible for each one, left Arlindo unable to give a confident answer despite having built every one of them personally. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about governing citizen-built low-code automations. Distinguish a documented, owned automation from an untracked one. Apply a method for maintaining a simple record of active automations and their owners. Recognise the signs that a growing set of automations needs a governance review. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 A Question Arlindo Could Not Confidently Answer Arlindo Nsue had built one automation after another for his NGO's finance team in Malabo over nearly two years, each one solving a genuine problem the day it went live. When a newly arrived finance director asked, in a routine planning meeting, exactly how many automations were currently running and who kept an eye on each one, Arlindo realised he genuinely could not answer with any confidence, despite having built every single one himself. 2.2 What Research Found About Governing Citizen-Built Automations Altus Viljoen, Marija Radic, Andreas Hein and colleagues drew on thirty interviews with citizen developers and low-code platform experts for a 2024 paper in MIS Quarterly Executive, examining what effective governance of citizen-built automations actually requires. Their finding was that entrusting automation building to people without formal governance in place risks the quiet accumulation of undocumented, unowned automations that eventually become a form of unmanaged technical debt. 2.3 Maintaining a Simple Record of Active Automations Recording What Each Automation Does and Who Owns It Keeping a simple, plainly written record of what each automation does, which apps it connects, and who is responsible for noticing if it breaks turns a scattered set of individually built tools into something an organisation can actually account for. Reviewing the Full List Periodically, Not Only When Something Breaks Setting a regular time to review the complete list of active automations, retiring ones no longer needed and reassigning ownership where it has quietly lapsed, catches drift before a new director's simple question exposes it all at once. 2.4 Key Practices Record what each automation does, which apps it connects, and who owns it. Review the full list of active automations on a regular schedule, not only when one breaks. Retire automations that no longer serve a real purpose rather than leaving them running unattended. Reassign ownership of an automation whenever its original owner changes roles or leaves. 2.5 A Worked Example: Arlindo's Automation Inventory Over the following two weeks, Arlindo built a simple inventory listing all fourteen automations he could identify, what each one did, which apps it touched, and who would now be responsible for noticing if it stopped working. Two of the fourteen turned out to be duplicating work another automation already handled, and one had been quietly failing for months without producing any output the finance team had ever actually used. The finance director's next planning meeting opened with Arlindo walking through the inventory directly, assigning a named owner to every remaining automation and a retirement date to the two duplicates. Arlindo's individual automations had each been built competently and had each solved a real problem in its moment. What had never existed was any single record connecting them, and only building that record ever let anyone, including Arlindo himself, actually account for what had accumulated. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Building automation after automation without ever recording what each one does or who owns it allows a genuinely useful set of tools to grow past the point where even its own builder can fully account for it, which is what left Arlindo without a confident answer to a routine question. Reviewing automations only when one visibly breaks, rather than on a regular schedule, lets duplicated or already-failing automations sit unnoticed until they happen to be discovered by accident. 2.7 Built Well Individually Is Not the Same as Governed Well Collectively Every one of Arlindo's fourteen automations had been built carefully and had solved a genuine problem when it was created. That individual care had never added up, on its own, to any organisation-wide account of what actually existed, and only a deliberate inventory ever turned fourteen separate efforts into something the finance team could genuinely rely on. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to maintain a documented, owned record of a growing set of automations rather than letting them accumulate untracked. This closes Course 101 and prepares you for Course 102, Automating Data Collection and Reporting Workflows, the next course in Pathway 54.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of the automations you or your team currently rely on. Could you name who owns each one and what would happen if it silently broke? 2. Build a simple inventory of every real automation you currently maintain, naming what each does, which apps it connects, and who owns it. Practical Output: Practical Output An automation inventory listing every real automation currently maintained, what each one does, which apps it connects, and a named owner for each. 7.0 References and Further Reading Viljoen, A., Radic, M., Hein, A., et al. quiz.q: Yohannes's automation produced a blank document on its first international, multi-item shipment. What did this reveal?
options: The logistics office's shipment records had been entered incorrectly
Ten successful runs of the same simple scenario are not the same kind of evidence as testing genuinely different scenarios
Customs paperwork should never be automated
The automation had been built using the wrong platform entirely
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Testing an Automation Against Edge Cases Before Trusting It Unattended) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to Parasuraman and Riley's 1997 research, what commonly happens once an automation has performed correctly several times?
options: People typically increase their monitoring of the automation further
People often over-rely on the automation, reducing the monitoring that would catch its failures
The automation becomes incapable of ever failing again
People stop using the automation entirely out of excess caution
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Testing an Automation Against Edge Cases Before Trusting It Unattended) before continuing.

quiz.q: What does this session recommend choosing test cases for?
options: Selecting only cases identical to the simplest, most common scenario
Selecting cases specifically because they differ from the simplest, most common scenario
Avoiding any test cases involving missing or unusual values
Testing a single case as many times as possible
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Testing an Automation Against Edge Cases Before Trusting It Unattended) before continuing.

quiz.q: Isatou's reminder automation ran without any error for three weeks while sending garbled appointment dates. What did this reveal?
options: The clinic's patients had misread their reminder texts
An automation can fail silently, completing without error while producing incorrect output
Appointment reminders should never be automated
The booking app itself had stopped working entirely
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 5 (Recognising When an Automation Has Silently Broken) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to van der Aalst, Bichler and Heinzl's 2018 research, why are automations built on another system's interface fragile?
options: They cannot be built using no-code platforms at all
They can fail when the underlying app changes something as minor as a date format, often without any visible error
They only fail when deliberately reprogrammed by a developer
They are fragile only when built by inexperienced automation builders
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 5 (Recognising When an Automation Has Silently Broken) before continuing.

quiz.q: What does this session recommend doing periodically with a critical automation?
options: Confirming only that it completed without an error message
Reading a sample of its actual recent output directly
Assuming its output is correct as long as it runs on schedule
Disabling it entirely to avoid any risk of silent failure
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 5 (Recognising When an Automation Has Silently Broken) before continuing.

Leave requests should never be automated
Erasto had entered the wrong supervisor's name into the system

options: The process automatically improves regardless of its original design
The process's existing flaws tend to be locked in place, sometimes at greater cost to fix later
Automation always removes the need for any human decision-making
Redesigning a process before automating it is unnecessary

options: Automating every step exactly as currently performed without question
Questioning whether each step still serves a real purpose
Skipping any consultation with people who perform the process
Assuming the process has no exceptions worth mapping
